formNote: Attach 잖아(요) straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; there is no 으 buffer, so a final consonant changes nothing (많다 to 많잖아요). For past events use 았/었잖아요 (말했잖아요), and a noun adds 이잖아요 / 잖아요 (주말이잖아요, 친구잖아요). The core job is to remind the listener of a fact you both already share, almost like saying 'come on, you know this' — it flags the reason as common ground rather than new news. Because it presumes the other person should already know, leaning on it too hard sounds mildly accusatory ('I already TOLD you'), which is why it is a friends-and-close-coworkers ending with no true 합니다 form. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for it to deliver fresh information ('나 어제 이사했잖아요' to someone who never knew you moved) — that lands as a passive-aggressive scold; for genuinely new background you want 거든요 instead.
usage: 았/었잖아 for a past event you both witnessed
That place is expensive, you know.
adjective stem + 잖아요, no 으 buffer
Fridays are always packed, you know.
pairs with 원래 to mean 'as we both know, by default'
examples: 야, 그 사람 너 좋아하잖아. 왜 모른 척해?
Dude, he likes you, you know. Why act clueless?
flags an open secret between close friends
오늘 팀장님 기분 안 좋잖아요. 보고는 내일 하죠.
The team lead's in a bad mood today, you know. Let's report tomorrow.
uses shared observation to justify a suggestion
배달비 또 올랐잖아. 그냥 가서 먹자.
Delivery fees went up again, you know. Let's just eat there.
both 알고 있는 사실로 결론을 끌어냄
mistakes: English speakers use 잖아요 to break news ('우리 헤어졌잖아요' to someone who didn't know) — but it presumes shared knowledge, so it sounds like a scolding 'as you should know.' For info the listener lacks, switch to 거든요 (헤어졌거든요).
Don't aim it at elders or strangers; even with 요 the 'you already know this' flavor reads as naggy or rude. Reserve it for friends and close colleagues, and soften with a gentle, not falling, tone.
It is not a yes/no question marker. 비싸잖아요? to ask 'isn't it expensive?' is unnatural — for confirmation use 비싸지 않아요? or 비싸죠?.

formNote: Add 거든(요) to a plain verb or adjective stem with no 으 buffer (작다 to 작거든요); past uses 았/었거든요 (잤거든요), and a noun adds 이거든요 (학생이거든요). It supplies a reason or piece of background the listener does NOT yet have — think of it as verbally opening a parenthesis: '(the thing is...)'. It frequently answers a 왜? or sets up the next sentence of a story, and the rising-then-settling intonation invites the listener to keep listening. The single most useful contrast for learners is 거든요 vs 잖아요: 거든요 delivers NEW information ('약속이 있거든요' = you didn't know I have plans), while 잖아요 recalls SHARED information ('약속 있다고 했잖아요' = I already told you). Said with a flat, clipped falling tone to a stranger it can sound a touch defensive or self-justifying, so let the pitch stay light.
usage: 저 오늘 못 가요. 약속이 있거든요.
I can't come today. I have plans, see.
supplies the unknown reason behind a refusal
그 카페 자주 가. 분위기가 좋거든.
I go to that cafe a lot. The vibe's great, see.
I didn't sleep last night, see.
Actually I'm vegetarian, just so you know.
pairs with 사실 to introduce fresh info
examples: 왜 이렇게 피곤해 보이냐고요? 어제 밤새 일했거든요.
Why do I look so tired? Because I pulled an all-nighter at work.
directly answers a 왜 with unknown context
저 이번 달은 좀 아껴야 돼요. 월세 올랐거든요.
I have to save this month. My rent went up, see.
거든요 sets up the reason for the first clause
그 사람한테 연락 안 해. 나 차였거든.
I'm not texting him. I got dumped, see.
반말, reveals a private reason as new info
mistakes: The number-one error is swapping 거든요 and 잖아요. 거든요 = the listener does NOT know yet; 잖아요 = you both already know. Telling a friend who already heard the news '나 차였거든' is fine as fresh disclosure, but if they witnessed it, 차였잖아 fits.
Don't use 거든요 as a neutral connector mid-sentence the way 아서/니까 work. It is sentence-final ('비싸거든요.'), not 'O 비싸거든 안 사요' — for a reason clause inside one sentence use 비싸서/비싸니까.
Avoid a hard, falling, clipped tone with strangers; '바쁘거든요!' snapped out sounds defensive, like 'because I'm busy, obviously.' Keep the pitch soft and informative.

formNote: Attach 더라고(요) to a plain verb or adjective stem to report something you personally witnessed, felt, or realized at an earlier moment and are now relaying — the 더 carries the meaning 'I retrieved this from my own past observation.' Crucially it marks firsthand evidence: you must have seen, heard, or directly experienced it, never merely been told. Because the discovery belongs to you, you normally avoid it for your OWN deliberate actions or feelings you already knew about (X 나 학생이더라고요), though it works beautifully for self-realizations you stumbled onto (혼자 살아 보니까 외롭더라고요 = I found out, to my surprise, that I'm lonely). Compare it with plain past 았/었어요, which just states a finished fact flatly; 더라고요 adds 'and this is what I noticed about it,' a reporter's color. The 고 is routinely dropped in speech, leaving the very casual 더라.
usage: When I went, it was better than I thought.
reports a firsthand impression after 가 보니까
The wait at that restaurant was really long.
The new hire is good at the job, I noticed.
observing a third person you watched directly
Living alone turned out to be lonely.
a self-realization you discovered, not knew
examples: 어제 소개팅 했는데 의외로 대화가 잘 통하더라고요.
I had a blind date yesterday, and we surprisingly clicked.
의외로 + 더라고요 frames an unexpected discovery
그 동네 가 봤는데 월세가 생각보다 싸더라고요.
I checked out that neighborhood; rent was cheaper than expected.
firsthand visit licenses 더라고요
회식 가 보니까 분위기가 생각보다 편하더라고요.
The company dinner turned out more relaxed than I expected.
reports a felt atmosphere you experienced
mistakes: Don't use 더라고요 for secondhand news you only heard. '친구가 시험 떨어졌더라고요' is odd if you weren't there — for hearsay use 떨어졌대요 (-대요). 더라고요 demands your own eyes/ears.
Avoid it for your own settled, already-known feelings or intentions: '나 너 좋아하더라고요' is wrong because you already knew. It only fits feelings you newly discovered in yourself (살아 보니 외롭더라고요).

It is past-leaning observation, so don't pair it with a clearly present-and-ongoing 'right now.' For what you see this second, use 보여요/네요 (비 와요 / 비 오네요), not 비 오더라고요, which implies you noticed it earlier.

formNote: Add ㄹ래요 after a vowel stem (가다 to 갈래요) and 을래요 after a consonant stem (먹다 to 먹을래요); ㄹ-final stems keep their single ㄹ and just add 래요 with no 으 buffer (놀다 to 놀래요, 만들다 to 만들래요). As a question it casually proposes doing something together or probes the listener's own will/preference; as a statement it declares your intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I feel like going). The sharp contrast to learn is ㄹ래요? vs ㄹ까요?: ㄹ까요? consults the other person's opinion on a shared plan ('shall we?', 같이 갈까요?), whereas ㄹ래요? asks what THEY personally want to do (같이 갈래요? = do you feel like going?), so it can sound a bit direct or even presumptuous to a superior. Because it centers the listener's raw will, polite as it is with 요, it is not deferential enough for a clear senior — there you upgrade to 가실래요? or 가시겠어요?.
examples: 주말에 시간 되면 영화 볼래?
If you're free this weekend, wanna catch a movie?
soft 반말 ask-out probing their willingness
점심 같이 시켜 먹을래요?
Wanna order delivery for lunch together?
consonant stem 먹을래요 in an office invite
오늘 한 잔 할래? 1차만 가볍게.
Wanna grab a drink today? Just one round, light.
한 잔 하다 collocation for casual drinking
mistakes: Don't fire ㄹ래요? at someone clearly above you; '부장님, 같이 갈래요?' asks the boss's bare preference and feels too forward. Upgrade to 같이 가실래요? or 같이 가시겠어요?.
ㄹ-final stems take only 래요 with no 으: 놀다 to 놀래요 (never 놀을래요), 만들다 to 만들래요 (never 만들을래요).

Don't confuse it with ㄹ까요?. 갈까요? consults a shared decision ('shall we go?'), while 갈래요? asks the listener's personal want. Using 갈래요? when you mean a joint 'shall we' can sound like you're pushing your plan onto them.

formNote: Verbs take 는데요 (가다 to 가는데요); adjectives take ㄴ데요 after a vowel (예쁘다 to 예쁜데요) and 은데요 after a consonant (좋다 to 좋은데요); 있다/없다 behave like verbs (재밌는데요) and the past for both is 았/었는데요 (재밌었는데요). Ending a sentence on 는데요 leaves the thought hanging open — it softens a statement, plants an unspoken 'but...,' or hands the conversational floor to the other person to react. Think of it as a half-finished bridge: you build the first span and let the listener walk across it. The crucial split for learners is the adjective rule: descriptive words must NOT take 는 (바쁜데요, not 바쁘는데요), because only action verbs and 있다/없다 use 는. Tonally, a trailing 는데요...? can convey surprise, mild pushback, or a polite hedge all at once depending on pitch, which is why it rarely stands fully alone with strangers without surrounding context.
usage: I'm kind of busy right now, though.
adjective 바쁘다 to 바쁜데요, soft refusal
I don't really know about that, though.
verb 모르다 to 모르는데요, polite hedge
examples: 그 사람 나쁘진 않은데요, 좀 제 스타일은 아니에요.
He's not bad, but he's just not my type.
는데요 sets up the gentle 'but' before the real point
디자인은 괜찮은데요, 마감일은 좀 무리일 것 같아요.
The design's fine, but the deadline seems tight.
softens office pushback by half-agreeing first
저 지금 카페에 있는데, 너 어디야?
I'm at the cafe right now, where are you?
는데 as a lead-in that invites a response
mistakes: Never put 는 on a plain adjective: it's 바쁜데요 / 좋은데요, not 바쁘는데요 / 좋는데요. Only verbs and 있다/없다 take the 는 form.

Don't mistake sentence-final 는데요 for the mid-sentence connector -는데. Here it deliberately trails off to imply more; '날씨가 좋은데요.' standing alone hints 'so shall we go out?' and needs context or a follow-up to land.

Watch the contrast 는데 vs 지만. Both mean 'but,' but 는데 sets a soft, open backdrop that invites continuation (좋은데 비싸요 = it's nice, and well, it's pricey...), while 지만 states a flatter, more clear-cut contrast (좋지만 비싸요 = it's nice but it's expensive). Overusing 지만 in chat sounds stiff.

english: I'm planning to / I intend to
formNote: Add 려고요 after a vowel stem (자다 to 자려고요) and 으려고요 after a consonant stem (모으다 to 모으려고요, 찾다 to 찾으려고요) to announce your own pre-formed intention, very often as a reply to '뭐 할 거예요?'. It is the relaxed, conversational clipping of 려고 해요, with the 해요 simply left implied. The contrast you must nail is 려고 vs 으러: both involve purpose, but 으러 attaches only to a movement verb to mark the goal of going/coming (사러 가요 = I go in order to buy), while 려고 states a standalone plan/aim and pairs with any verb (사려고요 = I'm planning to buy). A second caution: 려고요 reports the speaker's intention, so it is awkward to assert flatly about someone else's plan — for a third person's apparent intent you soften to 려나 봐요 or simply ask them.
usage: I'm just gonna rest at home today.
I'm trying to save up some money.
I'm planning to switch jobs next year.
examples: 이번 주말엔 소개팅 한번 나가 보려고요.
I'm thinking of trying a blind date this weekend.
나가 보다 + 려고요 softens to 'thinking of trying'
월세 너무 비싸서 좀 더 싼 데로 이사 가려고요.
Rent's too high, so I'm planning to move somewhere cheaper.
reason clause + intended action
오늘 회식은 1차만 가고 빠지려고요.
I'm planning to leave after the first round of the work dinner.
sequences plans with 가고 ... 빠지려고요
mistakes: Don't confuse 으려고 with 으러. Use 으러 only with go/come for the purpose of an errand (밥 먹으러 가요 = I go to eat); use 려고 for a standalone intention with any verb (밥 먹으려고요 = I'm planning to eat). '밥 먹으러요' as a full answer is wrong.
State it only about your own plans. For someone else's intention, '친구가 오려고요' sounds off — say 친구가 오려나 봐요 ('seems like my friend intends to come') or just report 온대요.
Don't graft a future ending on top: it's already forward-looking, so 자려고 할 거예요 is redundant. Say 자려고요 or, more fully, 자려고 해요.

formNote: Attach 는 중이에요 to a plain verb stem to stress that an action is actively unfolding at this very moment; ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 는 (만들다 to 만드는 중이에요, 살다 to 사는 중이에요). The Sino-Korean noun 中 (중) literally means 'the middle/midst,' so 가는 중 paints 'in the very midst of going.' With a bare noun you skip the verb form and say N 중이에요 (회의 중이에요 = mid-meeting, 공사 중 = under construction). The contrast to internalize is 는 중이에요 vs plain 고 있어요: 고 있어요 broadly marks ongoing or even habitual action (요즘 한국어 배우고 있어요 = I'm learning Korean these days), while 는 중이에요 zooms in on this single moment of being mid-task and resists habitual or stretched readings. Because it needs a real unfolding action, it rejects adjectives and stative verbs like 알다/있다 — there is no 아는 중이에요.
usage: I'm on my way right now.
I'm in the middle of eating.
I'm in the middle of working.
single ongoing task, not a habit
examples: 미안, 지금 일하는 중이라 이따 톡할게.
Sorry, I'm working right now, I'll text you later.
는 중이라 = 'because I'm mid-task' giving a reason
거의 다 왔어요, 지금 엘리베이터 타는 중이에요.
I'm almost there, getting in the elevator now.
pinpoints the action happening this second
다이어트 중이라 오늘은 치킨 패스할게.
I'm on a diet, so I'll pass on the chicken today.
noun 다이어트 + 중이라 for an ongoing state
mistakes: Don't attach it to adjectives or stative verbs: 아는 중이에요 / 예쁜 중이에요 are wrong because there's no unfolding action. For knowing a state, just say 알아요.
It marks the present midst, not the near future. 가는 중이에요 means 'I'm already en route,' NOT 'I'm about to leave.' For 'about to,' use 가려고요 or 곧 갈게요.
Don't overuse it for long-term, habitual things. 'These days I'm learning Korean' is 한국어 배우고 있어요, not 배우는 중이에요, which would oddly imply you're mid-lesson at this instant.

formNote: Verbs and 있다/없다 take 나 봐요 (오다 to 오나 봐요, 있다 to 있나 봐요); descriptive adjectives instead take ㄴ가/은가 봐요 (바쁘다 to 바쁜가 봐요, 좋다 to 좋은가 봐요), and nouns take 인가 봐요 (신입인가 봐요). The literal sense — 'I look (봐요) at whether (나)...' — captures that you are inferring from visible evidence, drawing a careful conclusion from something you observed rather than asserting it outright. The contrast learners need is 나 봐요 vs 겠어요/것 같아요: 겠어요 leans on gut feeling or general assumption (춥겠어요 = it must be cold, I imagine), and 것 같아요 is the all-purpose 'I think/seems,' while 나 봐요 specifically signals 'based on this clue in front of me, I gather...'. Since it is an outside guess, you don't apply it to your own clear feelings — 나 슬픈가 봐 (I guess I'm sad) only works as wry self-observation, never as a plain statement of how you feel.
usage: verb 오다 to 오나 봐요, inferring from a clue
Seems like those two are dating.
반말 나 봐, guessing from what you saw
adjective takes ㄴ가/은가 봐요, not 나 봐요
examples: 걔가 읽씹하네. 나한테 관심 없나 봐.
He left my message on read. Guess he's not into me.
없다 takes 없나 봐, conclusion from evidence
팀장님 아직 안 가셨네요. 마감 때문에 바쁜가 봐요.
The team lead hasn't left yet. Must be busy with the deadline.
adjective 바쁜가 봐요 inferred from an observed fact
다들 그 집 올리던데, 거기 핫플인가 봐요.
Everyone's posting that place; must be the new hotspot.
noun 핫플 + 인가 봐요 from social-media evidence
mistakes: Use ㄴ가/은가 봐요 for plain adjectives, not 나 봐요: 좋은가 봐요 / 바쁜가 봐요 (never 좋나 봐요 / 바쁘나 봐요). Verbs and 있다/없다 are the ones that take 나 봐요.
Don't use it about your own feelings you plainly know. '나 화났나 봐요' to report your own clear anger is odd; 나 봐요 is an outside-looking-in guess, fine only as ironic self-discovery.

Don't blur it with 겠어요. 비 오겠어요 is a forecast-style assumption ('it'll probably rain'); 비 오나 봐요 means you see a clue right now (wet ground, dark sky) and infer it's raining. Pick by whether you have present evidence.

formNote: Add ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel stem (늦다... wait, 늦다 is consonant — 넘어지다 to 넘어질 뻔했어요) and 을 뻔했어요 after a consonant stem (늦다 to 늦을 뻔했어요); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (울다 to 울 뻔했어요). It describes an event that very nearly occurred but ultimately did NOT — a near-miss or close call — and it is locked in the past tense 했어요 because the moment of almost-happening is already over. The defining nuance is the relief or alarm baked in: you escaped the outcome, so it usually pairs with a 살았다-style payoff (덕분에 살았어요, 겨우 피했어요) or a hair-raising setup. Don't confuse it with 을 것 같았어요 ('it seemed like it would'), which is a guess about likelihood; 뻔했어요 asserts the thing was a whisker away from really happening. The English trap is using it for things that DID happen — 'I almost finished' meaning you nearly completed it is NOT 끝낼 뻔했어요 (which would mean you came close but failed); for that, use 거의 끝냈어요.
usage: consonant stem 늦다 to 늦을 뻔했어요
반말 vowel stem 넘어지다 to 넘어질 뻔했어
ㄹ-stem 울다 drops ㄹ to 울 뻔했어요
examples: 지하철 놓칠 뻔했는데 겨우 탔어요.
I almost missed the subway but barely made it.
겨우 underscores the narrow escape
술 마시고 전 남친한테 연락할 뻔했잖아.
I almost texted my ex while drunk, you know.
combines with 잖아 to recall a shared close call
마감 깜빡할 뻔했는데 알림 덕분에 살았어요.
I almost forgot the deadline; the reminder saved me.
덕분에 살았어요 is the relief payoff
mistakes: It means the thing did NOT happen. If you actually missed the subway, don't say 놓칠 뻔했어요 (that means you nearly missed but caught it) — say 놓쳤어요.
Keep it fixed in the past: 늦을 뻔했어요, never 늦을 뻔해요 or 늦을 뻔할 거예요. The 'almost' moment is always already passed.
Don't use it for 'almost done / almost there' in the sense of near-completion. 'I'm almost finished' is 거의 다 했어요, not 끝낼 뻔했어요, which implies you nearly finished but didn't.

formNote: Present-tense verbs take 는 척하다 (자다 to 자는 척해요); descriptive adjectives take ㄴ/은 척하다 (예쁘다 to 예쁜 척해요, 괜찮다 to 괜찮은 척해요); and a completed past action takes 은/ㄴ 척하다 (듣다 to 들은 척하다 → 안 들은 척해요). The bound noun 척 means 'a put-on pose,' so the construction literally stages an act you don't truly feel or do — you perform the outside of a state without the inside. It carries a clear undertone of falseness or insincerity, which is why it pairs naturally with 그냥, 일부러, or 안 (그냥 못 본 척했어요). The near-twin 체 (못 본 체했어요) means the same thing with a slightly bookish, old-fashioned flavor; in everyday speech 척 dominates. The English-speaker pitfall is matching the wrong modifier: 'pretend to be pretty' is 예쁜 척 (adjective form), never 예쁘는 척, and 'pretend not to hear' as a past act is 못 들은 척, not 못 듣는 척.
usage: present verb 자다 to 자는 척
I pretended I didn't hear it.
past action 듣다 to 들은 척
examples: 전 남친 마주쳤는데 그냥 못 본 척하고 지나갔어.
I ran into my ex and just walked past pretending not to see him.
못 본 척 = past 보다, the most common collocation
회식에서 안 취한 척했는데 사실 엄청 취했어요.
I acted sober at the work dinner but I was actually wasted.
안 취한 척 contrasts the fake outside with the real state
부장님 농담에 다들 재밌는 척 웃었어요.
Everyone laughed like the boss's joke was funny.
재밌다 is 있다-type, so 재밌는 척
mistakes: Match the modifier to the word class: verbs use 는 척 (자는 척), adjectives use ㄴ/은 척 (예쁜 척), and a finished past action uses 은/ㄴ 척 (들은 척). 예쁘는 척 or 못 듣은 척 are wrong forms.
It implies the act is fake, so don't use it when something is genuinely true. If you really are fine, say 괜찮아요, not 괜찮은 척해요, which would mean you're faking it.

Distinguish 안 본 척 from 못 본 척. 못 본 척 = pretend you COULDN'T see (didn't notice), the natural choice for dodging your ex; 안 본 척 = pretend you didn't look on purpose, a different and less idiomatic nuance here.
